summary: Reviewed the DVPWA (Damn Vulnerable Python Web App) aiohttp application: DAO/SQL layer, views/routing, authentication and session utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 templates, and configuration. The app is deliberately vulnerable and confirms it: a classic SQL injection in Student.create, application-wide disabling of Jinja2 autoescaping (stored XSS), unsalted MD5 password hashing, CSRF protection commented out, sessions cookies without HttpOnly, and a missing authorization check on the admin-only 'evaluate' endpoint. Coverage was the Python source, templates, migrations and config; static JS/CSS assets were not reviewed.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via Python string formatting
findings.description: Student.create builds an INSERT statement by interpolating the untrusted 'name' value directly into the SQL string with Python's % operator instead of using a parameterized query. The value flows from the unauthenticated POST /students/ handler (views.students -> data['name']) straight into this query, so any anonymous visitor can inject arbitrary SQL. Because psycopg/aiopg can execute batched statements, an attacker can break out of the VALUES('...') context (e.g. name = x'); DROP TABLE marks; --) to read or modify any table, including the users/pwd_hash table.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}) ... await cur.execute(q)  # name comes from views.students: await Student.create(conn, data['name'])
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query like every other DAO method: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/format/f-strings from user input.

findings.title: Stored XSS from application-wide autoescape=False in Jinja2 setup
findings.description: Jinja2 is initialized with autoescape=False, so every template variable is rendered as raw HTML unless a developer remembers to add '| e'. Several templates render attacker-controlled data without escaping: course.jinja2 renders review.review_text (line 22), course.title and course.description (lines 14-15), and student names (line 19, 49). review_text is fully user-supplied via POST /courses/{id}/review and student name via POST /students/, so an attacker can store <script> payloads that execute in any viewer's browser (including the admin). Combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie, this yields session theft.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli', 'templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)  # then course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }} rendered unescaped; review_text stored via Review.create from views.review
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, or select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) so escaping is the default, and treat '| safe' as the explicit opt-out. Do not rely on per-variable '| e'.

findings.title: Passwords stored and verified as unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to a plain unsalted MD5 of the supplied password, and the fixtures store credentials the same way (migrations/001-fixtures.sql lines 10-13, e.g. md5('superadmin')). MD5 is fast and unsalted, so any leaked pwd_hash (reachable through the SQL injection above) is trivially reversible with rainbow tables/brute force, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. This directly compromises the admin account.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  # fixtures: VALUES ('Super', NULL, 'Admin', 'superadmin', md5('superadmin'), TRUE)
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 (e.g. passlib or hashlib.scrypt) and compare with a constant-time function. Migrate stored hashes on next login.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled (csrf_middleware not registered)
findings.description: The application defines a working CSRF middleware (middlewares.csrf_middleware) that validates a per-session token, but it is commented out of the middleware chain, so no POST endpoint verifies the _csrf_token. All state-changing routes (login on /, create student, create course, submit review, evaluate/grade student, logout) accept cross-site forged requests. An attacker page can, for example, silently submit reviews or grades on behalf of a logged-in admin.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware,\n error_middleware,]  # csrf_middleware exists in middlewares.py:26 but is never applied
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure all POST forms include {{ csrf_token() }} (the review form already does).

findings.title: Missing authorization check on grade-submission (evaluate) endpoint
findings.description: The evaluate handler creates a Mark (student grade) but performs no authentication or authorization. The UI only exposes the evaluate form to admins (course.jinja2 gates it behind auth_user.is_admin), implying it is an admin-only action, but the backend route POST /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} has no @authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator. Any anonymous user can POST valid points (0-5) and insert arbitrary grades for any student/course. The authorize() helper exists but is only applied to logout.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  # no get_auth_user/authorize; contrast @authorize() on logout (views.py:156)
findings.recommendation: Decorate evaluate with @authorize(ensure_admin=True) (and add appropriate auth to the students/courses creation handlers), enforcing access control server-side rather than only hiding UI.

findings.title: Session cookies issued without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: The Redis session storage is constructed with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Given the stored XSS above (autoescape disabled), an injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack accounts, including the admin session. No Secure flag is set either, allowing interception over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Use the default httponly=True and add secure=True (serve over HTTPS). Only disable HttpOnly if JS genuinely needs the cookie, which it does not here.
